items.title: Headlines for November 05, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Vance Blames Republican Election Losses on the U.S. War on Iran Nov 05, 2026 Democrats are continuing to build on historic gains in U.S. midterm elections, as late returns show Tuesday’s blue wave could rival Democrats’ sweep of the 1974 elections that followed the Watergate scandal. When the 120th Congress convenes in January, Democrats will control both chambers of Congress for the first time in four years. And this time, they’ll have significantly larger majorities. In the House, Democrats have won at least 240 seats compared to 147 for Republicans, with four dozen races yet to be called. Democrats are projected to surpass 250 seats in the House. In the Senate, the Democratic caucus will grow to at least 54 senators, with two races — Alaska and Mississippi — too close to call. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan by just 637 votes, with nearly a quarter of ballots yet to be counted. Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system means it could take days or weeks to determine the winner. Mississippi’s Senate race remains dramatically close, with the latest numbers showing Democrat Scott Colom ahead of incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 1,100 votes. Colom is now favored to win, as only a few thousand provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots remain to be counted. In a lengthy social media post, Vice President JD Vance blamed historic Republican election losses squarely on the war on Iran. Vance wrote, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.” On Wednesday, reporters asked President Trump about Vance’s comments. > Reporter: “Mr. President, Vice President Vance says the reason Republicans lost the war — lost last night was the war in Iran.” > President Donald Trump: “Well, I think it’s largely true, because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term. And probably that’s — probably it’s true. But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again, because, long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” President Trump held his post-election news conference outside the White House ballroom he’s building, signing one of the beams. Iran’s leadership responded to the U.S. election with a warning that any renewed attacks would draw a far wider response. A written statement attributed to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei argued Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz had shattered the “myth of America’s invincibility.” ... ## Yemeni Government Claims to Have Thwarted Large-Scale Attack by Ansar Allah in Taiz Nov 05, 2026 In Yemen, forces loyal to the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government say they’ve fended off a large-scale attack by Ansar Allah fighters in Taiz governate. The violence added to a growing humanitarian crisis in the city of Taiz, where residents are short on water, food, fuel and medical supplies. On Wednesday, the Red Cross said it had delivered four truckloads of essential goods to Taiz. That’s a tiny fraction of what’s needed. The United Nations is urging Yemen’s warring parties to fully reopen roads into Taiz. This is a U.N. spokesperson. > Stéphane Dujarric: “Taiz, which is home to around 1 million human beings, roads are closed, and supplies are running out. Water production has been cut in half. Food prices have soared by at least 50% on the market in Taiz city. And hospitals are running out of fuel, and they are running out of medicine. The situation is critical, to say the least.” ## Israeli Attacks Kill at Least Four Palestinians in Gaza ... In the Gaza Strip, Al Jazeera is reporting that Israeli military gunfire ... Israeli attacks have killed at least four Palestinians so far today. ... ## World Health Organization Approves Trials of Two New Ebola Vaccines The World Health Organization has approved trials of two new vaccines built specifically for the latest deadly strain of Ebola. The virus has killed more than 5,300 people since May, most of them in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in the largest outbreak in the country’s history. The latest strain of Ebola kills about half of those infected. This Meg Doherty, a director at the World Health Organization. > Dr. Meg Doherty: “We’re looking for early results, we hope, in early 2027, so that we can then start to be thinking realistically about that post-trial access and using these vaccines in the countermeasures and really helping to save lives, stop onward infections and help bring the overall epidemic to an end.”

items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 5, 2026
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Thursday, including US President Donald Trump defending the Iran war amid midterm losses, world leaders offering mixed reactions to Democrats' victory in US midterm elections, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps saying two oil tankers and a tugboat catching fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. US President Donald Trump said the war in Iran was worth the political and economic costs as his Republic Party lost the midterm elections, insisting that the country had "no choice" but to take military action to prevent Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons. Asked at the White House whether he believed the conflict was worth it, Trump responded: “I do. Yeah. I mean, well, you have no choice.” “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” he added. Asked about Vice President JD Vance's suggestion that the war in Iran contributed to Republican losses, Trump agreed, acknowledging that the conflict had pushed gasoline prices higher in the short term. “Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up,” he said. Meanwhile Vance blamed the war with Iran for Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections, saying voter anger over the conflict drove former Trump supporters to back Democrats.

items.title: Barkin sees interest rate hikes ahead, but at a gradual pace
items.excerpt: Published Thu, Nov 5 2026 9:29 AM EST Updated 23 Min Ago ... Key Points - Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further - A gradual rate of increases "makes sense," Barkin said. - Inflation "is the most important risk right now," and artificial intelligence is pushing prices up, he said. Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further, though he's not sure by how much or at what pace. In a CNBC interview that was part of the Richmond Fed's 2026 CFO Summit, the policymaker expressed concern over inflation and said monetary policy will need to adjust. "Unemployment's near record lows, and inflation is too high. That means the path is pretty straightforward. The question, of course, is pace," Barkin said in the talk with CNBC's Steve Liesman. "Gradual makes sense if you think there's uncertainty in the world, and if you think that there's information you're going to get in the period. And I think that's still a pace that makes sense to me," he added. Barkin's comments come a little more than a week after his colleagues voted to keep the Fed's benchmark overnight borrowing rate anchored in a range between 3.75% and 4%. While Barkin is not a voting member on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee now, he will be in 2027. In its post-meeting statement, the FOMC said it is awaiting the "accumulation of more information" as it deliberates where to go next. When the committee OK'd a quarter percentage point hike in September, officials largely agreed that another increase was likely before the end of 2026. Markets are pricing in a better than 80% chance of a hike in December, then one more move in 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Barkin said he considers current policy close to a point where it neither restricts nor promotes growth, which officials consider a neutral rate. ... "If you're restricting the economy, presumably you're restricting consumption, which is you know roughly two-thirds of the economy, and that's relatively elevated," he said. "So that would make the case that we're a little bit accommodative." Inflation, he added, "is the most important risk right now ... and I hope that our move in September and whatever else we might choose to do in the future will have some impact on inflation." Artificial intelligence is one source of price pressures, though he said it eventually will spur production and help ease inflation further down the road.

items.title: Here's what the Democratic election rout could mean for the U.S. economy
items.excerpt: The Democratic midterm election sweep could result in changes in economic policies related to trade, spending priorities and artificial intelligence. But the biggest forces shaping the economy aren't going to change just because the party in power did. Affordability pressures, heavy levels of government spending and growth that is dependent on the artificial intelligence tail wind are likely to persist, economists say. And all of those factors pose risks to the economy. "It's in a very kind of fragile place, and I don't know that it would take a lot to push the economy off the rails, and recession becomes a much greater risk," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "That isn't the case at the moment, but I don't think that's gone away." Zandi said he had been worried before the election that the economy was under threat from inflation, an underwhelming labor market and geopolitical dangers, and remains concerned now. ... "I don't expect any change in economic policy. The Iran war, the tariffs and trade policy, the heavy-handed immigration policy, all are done under executive order. They're not legislatively driven," Zandi said. "The president thought they were good policies before the election. I don't know why he'd change his mind after the election," Zandi added. "So I think they will continue to be policies that restrain growth and add to inflationary pressures and interest rates." Zandi sees the AI hyperscaler buildout as a key to economic growth, but also a source of potential peril. "The risks are decidedly to the downside because the growth is so dependent on AI, and the AI growth effects are so dependent on the equity market, and the equity market is so dependent on the valuations," he said. "It just feels like kind of a very fragile place, and the labor market is not well functioning." ... ## Two economies The election happened amid a dichotomy in economic views. Top-line numbers such as gross domestic product, consumer spending and the unemployment rate tell the story of an economy growing briskly while consumers spend and most Americans who want jobs are at work. GDP accelerated at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter while consumer spending grew 3.8%. The unemployment rate is at 4.2% while layoffs are around their lowest level since 1969. However, rising prices have overshadowed those otherwise solid metrics. The inflation rate in September as judged by the consumer price index was 3.7% — up sharply from 2.3% in April 2025 when Trump announced an aggressive round of so-called reciprocal tariffs against U.S. trading partners. The Iran war has only aggravated those conditions. The CPI was at just 2.4% when the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February, a war that has caused gas prices to soar. And wages aren't keeping up with rising costs. Wage growth when adjusted for inflation has turned negative, down 0.7% from a year ago in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

items.title: What Millions of Data Points Reveal About US Inflation
items.excerpt: In ... The BPP’s topline metric shows why Americans are feeling squeezed, with a headline reading of 4.4% in September, above the official Consumer Price Index print of 3.7%. But a closer look into the data shows price pressures more localized than in past inflation waves, and with disinflationary forces in play, too. Economists often focus on the “trimmed mean,” which excludes the outliers. It’s a measure Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has praised. The Cleveland Fed’s trimmed-mean calculation — widely followed among economists — groups products into 45 aggregates before excluding the extremes. The BPP makes it possible to cull the outliers at the level of over 30,000 individual products, providing a more granular picture. The BPP’s trimmed mean shows the underlying pace of inflation at 2.2% through October. That’s already close to the Fed’s 2% target and below the 2.7% reported by the Cleveland Fed, whose data run through September.

items.title: How Trump lost control of Congress and Musk’s Texas businesses brace for blue wave: Morning Rundown
items.excerpt: ## Democrats won on affordability. What happens next? After more than 80% of midterm voters said they were worried about the price of necessities, a “blue tsunami” came through for Democrats who pledged to make life more affordable. Now comes the daunting task of turning this promise into a reality. Congressional Democrats will have several policies they can pursue to push down consumer costs — assuming they make it past Trump, who has the power to veto any legislation Congress passes. Incoming leaders, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Texas’ James Talarico, and party mainstays, like Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, have pushed ideas such as Medicare for All, free preschool and reversing Republican cuts to healthcare. But Trump’s own policies — and Republicans’ lackluster midterm results — serve as a cautionary tale for Democrats as they attempt to address affordability.

items.title: Democrats vow to rein in Trump as he shows off White House ballroom By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Democrats vowed to use their resounding midterm victory to rein in President Donald Trump, setting up two years of possible deadlock in Washington, as Trump spent his first post-election appearance showing off his under-construction White House ballroom. A wave of anger over Trump’s policies, particularly the US-Iran war’s role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54-44. Democrats also gained at least 30 seats in the House of Representatives. It will be the first time that Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Wednesday that the incoming majority would be focused on affordability and accountability. ... The Alaska race may not be called for more than a week because of ranked-choice tabulation, while the timeline for a decision in Mississippi remained unclear. Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise. The Democratic victory is fueling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court’s two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its ​conservative majority. In the meantime, Republicans hold the reins and will have at least one must-pass piece of legislation ahead – a measure to fund the federal government past December – that they could use to enact conservative priorities during the so-called lame-duck period.

She said the new project is still in development and will follow her successful 2022 release, “SOS” which saw a deluxe edition added in 2024. ... This October 31 broadcast surpassed the previous season high of 4.6 million viewers from the season opener, which featured Jalen Brunson as host. ... Maya Hawke will anchor an ensemble cast in a live action “Magic: The Gathering” movie. Legendary Entertainment and Hasbro Entertainment are producing.
